slots.practicalActivity: Write out the five Salesforce ecosystem roles (Administrator, Platform App Builder, Developer, Consultant, Architect) from memory, in order, with one sentence per role naming which role's skills it builds on. Then write one paragraph locating yourself: which of the two destinations — Salesforce Data Analyst or Salesforce Technical Architect — sounds like the work you want next, and why, based on everything you built in the LTV Customer Management System capstone.
slots.deliverable: A written five-role map with build-on relationships, plus a one-paragraph statement of which destination you're leaning toward and why.

slots.practicalActivity: Take one real deliverable from your LTV Customer Management System capstone and write it twice — once as a vague, generic bullet and once using the action + artifact + tool pattern (a real number, a real deliverable, a real Salesforce tool). Then draft your full one-page resume following the lesson's six-section structure, pulling 3-4 capstone deliverables (the data model, the security model, a Flow, a validation rule, the dashboard) into bullets written in that pattern, and listing only certifications you've actually earned.
slots.deliverable: A real one-page draft resume with a capstone/projects section written entirely in the action + artifact + tool pattern.

slots.practicalActivity: Open your own Trailhead profile settings and set visibility to Public if it isn't already. Fill in About Me with a short, honest line naming your focus (for example, "Salesforce Administrator, Flow automation, data security"), then list the three badges, trails, or Superbadges on your profile most relevant to an Administrator role, and add your profile link to the resume header you drafted last slot.
slots.deliverable: A Public Trailhead profile with a completed About Me line, a written list of your three most relevant badges/trails/Superbadges, and the profile URL added to your resume.

slots.practicalActivity: Draft the outline for your own LTV Customer Management System portfolio page: one line per section — the business problem, data model, security model, automation, validation and data quality, reports and dashboards — with a placeholder note for which screenshot goes in each section. Decide and write down where you'll host it (a Google Doc, a Notion page, a simple site, or a PDF), and confirm it will contain no live credentials or security tokens.
slots.deliverable: A written portfolio-page outline with all six sections placeholder-noted for screenshots, plus a stated hosting choice.

slots.practicalActivity: Install the Salesforce CLI (`npm install -g @salesforce/cli`), run `sf org login web` to connect it to your Trailhead Playground or Developer Edition org from the capstone, then run `sf template generate project` to scaffold a source-driven project and `sf project retrieve start` to pull one real piece of metadata (a custom object or Flow from your capstone) into it. Confirm the default `.gitignore` excludes your local auth directories before committing anything.
slots.deliverable: A local source-driven Salesforce DX project containing one real retrieved metadata item from your capstone, with the auth-excluding `.gitignore` intact, ready to push to a GitHub repository.

slots.practicalActivity: Find and join one real Trailblazer Community Group in your region or specialty area. Write down one real question you could answer on the Feed in an area close to your capstone work (security, Flow automation, or data management), draft an answer to it, and add your Trailhead profile and portfolio links to your Community profile.
slots.deliverable: Membership in one real Trailblazer Community Group, a drafted real Feed answer, and a Community profile with your Trailhead and portfolio links added.

slots.practicalActivity: Assemble this chapter's five pieces into one consistent job-search presence: cross-check that the report count, object count, and Flow count you wrote on your resume match exactly what's described in your portfolio outline and what's actually retrievable from your org. Fix any mismatch now, then link your resume, Trailhead profile, and portfolio to each other in both directions.
slots.deliverable: A consistency-checked presence package — resume, Trailhead profile, portfolio outline, and GitHub project — with matching numbers and working cross-links between all four.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the realistic certification sequence for both destinations from the lesson: the shared Administrator/App Builder foundation, then either the Developer-to-Architect track or the Data Analyst track. Apply the lesson's three readiness questions to yourself honestly: can you rebuild core Administrator objectives hands-on in a Playground without a guide open, did your capstone already cover a meaningful share of them, and are you treating practice exams as a readiness check rather than your study plan itself.
slots.deliverable: A written certification-sequence map for your chosen destination, plus honest written answers to the three readiness questions for the Administrator credential specifically.

lessons.title: Study Plans for Administrator and App Builder

slots.practicalActivity: Open your LTV Customer Management System capstone and map each object, security decision, and automation you built to a rough exam domain (data model, security, automation, or reporting), following the lesson's lab. For whichever domain feels thinnest, go back into your Developer Edition org right now and rebuild one piece of it hands-on with no guide open, to confirm you actually understand it rather than just remembering it.
slots.deliverable: A written domain-mapping table of your capstone work against the Administrator exam's rough topic areas, plus a note on which domain you rebuilt hands-on and what it confirmed.

lessons.title: Study Plans for Developer and Architect Credentials

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph study plan for whichever track matches the destination you leaned toward in Lesson 1 — the Developer-to-Architect track, or hold this lesson's Architect-domain framing in mind for later if you're leaning toward the Data Analyst destination instead. If pursuing the Developer track, use the `sf` CLI workflow from the GitHub lesson to retrieve one more piece of metadata and write down what a unit test for it would need to check.
slots.deliverable: A written one-paragraph study plan for your chosen next-credential track, naming the specific Trailhead-catalog credential by its real current name.

slots.practicalActivity: Go to trailhead.salesforce.com/credentials directly right now and find the exact current name, "About the Exam" page, question count, time limit, and passing score for the specific credential you're targeting next. Write today's date next to what you found, as a record that you verified it yourself rather than trusting this course's or any other source's possibly-outdated description.
slots.deliverable: A dated, written record of the real current exam details (name, format, passing score) for your target credential, verified directly on Trailhead's live site.

slots.practicalActivity: Combine the last four lessons into one finished personal certification study plan: your chosen first credential (verified by its real current name), your domain-mapping table against your capstone, one specific weak area you're going to rebuild hands-on before scheduling, and a realistic target exam date.
slots.deliverable: A one-page personal certification study plan naming a specific credential, a weak-area rebuild commitment, and a target exam date.

slots.practicalActivity: Go back through your LTV Customer Management System capstone and write out four real, specific answers: a migration/data-loading decision, a security-model decision (why these OWD settings, why this sharing rule), a growth story (something you now understand because you had to build it), and a pushback story (where the easy configuration would have broken a best practice). Then write out, in the correct troubleshooting order, how you'd answer "a user can't see a record they should see" — object/field access, OWD, role hierarchy/sharing rules, manual/Apex sharing.
slots.deliverable: Four written, capstone-specific interview answers plus a correctly-ordered written troubleshooting answer to the record-visibility scenario question.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, in your own words, why governor limits exist (multi-tenancy, not an arbitrary number), and explain bulkification and trigger recursion as the two classic trigger bugs, including the real fix for each. Write one honest sentence stating exactly what Lightning Web Components experience you actually have versus what you don't, in the lesson's recommended "here's what I've built, here's what I haven't yet" style.
slots.deliverable: Written explanations of governor limits, bulkification, and trigger recursion with their fixes, plus one honest LWC-experience statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a structured answer to "how do you gather requirements?" following the lesson's five steps (identify stakeholders, run discovery, document requirements, prioritize, validate). Then write out how you'd respond, in a client's own terms (cost, risk, maintainability, future flexibility), if a client asked for something that broke a Salesforce best practice — naming the specific downside and an alternative that still meets their real need.
slots.deliverable: A written five-step requirements-gathering answer and a written best-practice-pushback response using the client's own language.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the lesson's fictional "Cascadia Outdoor Supply" scenario (three Salesforce orgs from acquisitions plus a legacy ERP, wanting one customer view with no processing downtime) using the four-step approach: write the clarifying questions you'd ask first, state the assumptions you'd make if they weren't answered, propose one direction with its tradeoff named explicitly, and name one security/scale consideration you'd raise unprompted.
slots.deliverable: A written four-part response to the Cascadia Outdoor Supply scenario: clarifying questions, stated assumptions, one proposed direction with a named tradeoff, and one unprompted security/scale note.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's six-step structure, sketch (on paper, a whiteboard, or any drawing tool) a design for the fictional "Fairmont Logistics" scenario: clarify the requirement, sketch Shipment/Customer objects and relationships, add the security model (driver visibility by assignment), add the integration touchpoint (inbound API or platform event), add automation, and talk through what changes at large scale. Narrate it out loud while you draw, timed, as if presenting to a panel.
slots.deliverable: A labeled Fairmont Logistics whiteboard sketch covering all six structure steps, plus a timed recording or notes from narrating it out loud.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a timed, out-loud mock interview (recorded, or with a study partner) combining this chapter's Administrator, Developer, and Consultant material: deliver your record-visibility troubleshooting answer, your governor-limits/bulkification explanation, and your requirements-gathering answer back to back, as if moving through an Administrator interview, then a Developer interview, then a Consultant interview in the same day.
slots.deliverable: A recording or witnessed notes from a timed mock interview covering Administrator, Developer, and Consultant question styles back to back.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a second timed mock session focused entirely on the Architect-level material: present your Cascadia Outdoor Supply answer out loud, then have a study partner (or record yourself and play devil's advocate) push back with at least two follow-up questions. Separately, re-draw and narrate the Fairmont Logistics whiteboard from a cold start, without looking at your earlier notes.
slots.deliverable: Recorded or witnessed notes from a timed Architect-style mock round including at least two follow-up pushback questions, plus one cold, unaided whiteboard re-draw.

slots.practicalActivity: Write all three versions of your capstone presentation named in the lesson — the under-a-minute recruiter version, the decisions-and-tradeoffs hiring-manager version, and the full-detail technical-panel version — following the five-part structure (business problem, solution design, decisions that mattered, the result, what you'd do differently at scale). Practice the technical-panel version out loud, narrating while you click through your actual org, with a screenshot backup ready in case the live demo breaks.
slots.deliverable: Three written capstone-presentation scripts (recruiter, hiring-manager, technical-panel lengths) plus a practiced, narrated live-org run-through with a screenshot backup set.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick three real decisions from your capstone (why you set OWD the way you did, why one piece of logic became a validation rule instead of a Flow, why one report or dashboard component exists) and write out each one using the option/reason/cost framework — what you chose, why over the alternative, and what it costs. Then write your own answer to "what would you do differently?" for one of them, framed as a scale/hindsight tradeoff, not a confession.
slots.deliverable: Three written option/reason/cost explanations of real capstone decisions, plus one written "what would you do differently" answer framed around scale.

lessons.title: Your First 90 Days in a Salesforce Role

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own personal 30/60/90-day plan for a first Salesforce Administrator role, following the lesson's arc: what you'd specifically do in the first 30 days to learn the org before touching it, what kind of small, visible "quick win" you'd target in days 30-60, and what it would look like to own something end to end and propose one improvement by day 90.
slots.deliverable: A written personal 30/60/90-day plan naming a specific quick-win type and a specific end-to-end ownership goal.

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the full credential ladder from where you are now toward Certified Technical Architect (Developer, then the Architect domain credentials, then the Application/System Architect milestones, then the CTA review board), and separately write one honest paragraph on which of the two forking ladders — Data & Analytics Architect or Technical Architect — matches what energized you most in this program, and why.
slots.deliverable: A written CTA credential ladder and a one-paragraph, reasoned choice between the Data & Analytics Architect and Technical Architect ladders.

slots.practicalActivity: Assemble the complete job-search package this course produced: the resume, the Public Trailhead profile, the portfolio outline, the GitHub project, the certification study plan, and your three capstone presentation scripts. Cross-check every number and claim across all six pieces one final time for consistency.
slots.deliverable: A single assembled, internally consistent job-search package covering resume, Trailhead profile, portfolio, GitHub project, certification plan, and presentation scripts.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a half-page closing reflection on the full 9-month Salesforce Administrator program: what you built across Salesforce Foundations, Administration, Declarative Development, the LTV Customer Management System capstone, and this career-preparation course; which ladder — Data & Analytics Architect or Technical Architect — you're choosing to pursue next; and your first concrete job-search action for next week (one specific job posting to apply to, or one specific Trailblazer Community Group meeting to attend).
slots.deliverable: A half-page written program reflection naming your next-ladder choice and one concrete, dated job-search action for the coming week.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: Closes the full 9-month Salesforce Administrator program with a complete, consistency-checked job-search package — a resume, a Public Trailhead profile, a narrative portfolio, a GitHub-committed capstone project, a verified certification study plan, and rehearsed Administrator, Developer, Consultant, and Architect-style interview answers built from the LTV Customer Management System capstone — ready to apply for Salesforce Administrator roles immediately.
